parts.latex:
A cricket is an insect. The male cricket produces a chirping sound.

A scientist wants to explore the relationship between the temperature in degrees Celsius and the number of cricket chirps heard in a 15-second time interval.

Once a day for 20 days, the scientist collects data. Based on the 20 data points, the scientist provides the information below.

\begin{itemize}
\item A box-plot of the temperature data is shown.

\exfigure{34_q27_1}
\item The mean temperature in the dataset is $0.525^\circ\text{C}$ below the median temperature in the dataset.
\item A total of 684 chirps was counted when collecting the 20 data points.
\end{itemize}

The scientist fits a least-squares regression line using the data $(x,y)$, where $x$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $y$ is the number of chirps heard in a 15-second time interval. The equation of this line is

$$y=-10.6063+bx,$$

where $b$ is the slope of the regression line.

The least-squares regression line passes through the point $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$ where $\bar{x}$ is the sample mean of the temperature data and $\bar{y}$ is the sample mean of the chirp data.

Calculate the number of chirps expected in a 15-second interval when the temperature is $19^\circ$ Celsius. Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.
parts.note: Least-squares regression with box-plot data: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{x} &= 22 - 0.525 \\ &= 21.475 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \bar{y} &= \dfrac{684}{20} \\ &= 34.2 \end{aligned}$$
Substituting $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ into the regression equation, we have
$$\begin{aligned} 34.2 &= -10.6063 + b(21.475) \\ \dfrac{44.8063}{21.475} &= b \\ b &= 2.08644\ldots \end{aligned}$$
When $x = 19$,
$$\begin{aligned} y &= -10.6063 + 2.08644\ldots \times 19 \\ &= 29.03606\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ 29 chirps are expected.
criteria: Finds value of $b$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$ into the regression equation, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ and $\bar{y}$, or equivalent merit
Finds the value of $\bar{x}$ or $\bar{y}$ or the median of the temperature, or equivalent merit

283.stem:
Last month eight houses were sold in Greenvale.

The selling prices of the houses were:

$$\begin{gathered} \$480\,000\quad \$505\,000\quad \$517\,000\quad \$528\,000\\ \$528\,000\quad \$552\,000\quad \$580\,000\quad \$980\,000 \end{gathered}$$

parts.latex: Show that the value of the most expensive house sold is an outlier for this data set.
parts.note: Quartiles, IQR and outliers of a data set are not in the 2024 Advanced course

parts.latex: Explain the effect of the outlier on the mean and median selling prices for this data set. Justify your answer with relevant calculations.
parts.note: Summary statistics of a data set (mean, median, outliers) are not in the 2024 Advanced course

solutions.latex:
$$Q_1=511\,000,\quad Q_3=566\,000$$

$$\begin{aligned}IQR&=566\,000-511\,000\\ &=55\,000\end{aligned}$$

$$1.5\times IQR=82\,500$$

Upper bound for outlier is $566\,000+82\,500=648\,500$.

$980\,000>648\,500$, hence the most expensive house sold is an outlier.

With the outlier present, median is $\$528\,000$ and mean is $\$583\,750$.

With the outlier removed, median is $\$528\,000$ and mean is $\$527\,143$ (to the nearest dollar).

The presence of the outlier significantly increases the mean without any change in the median.
criteria: Provides correct explanation without justification, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct explanation justified with relevant calculations

parts.latex: $$\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{\sin 2x}{3x}=$$
parts.note: Limit sin x / x as x -> 0: not in 2024 Advanced.

solutions.latex:
Use
$$\lim_{\theta \to 0}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta} = 1$$

$$\begin{aligned} \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{\sin 2x}{3x} &= \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{2}{3}\cdot\dfrac{\sin 2x}{2x} \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3}\times 1 \\ &= \dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: cumulative frequency graph of chess game duration (minutes), 15 to 180, cumulative frequency to 80

Frequency tables and histograms.evidence: Read across from cumulative frequency 20 to the curve, then down
Frequency tables and histograms.reason: Reading the cumulative frequency graph is the method; kept as unsure (a quartile is also involved).

solutions.latex:
75% of games took more than $n$ minutes, so 25% took at most $n$ minutes:
$$25\%\times80=20\text{ games}$$
Read across from cumulative frequency $20$ to the curve, then down. The point lies halfway between $(60,15)$ and $(75,25)$:
$$n=60+\dfrac{20-15}{25-15}\times15=67.5$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the school key gave D ($112.5$), which answers "75% took LESS than $n$ minutes". The question says MORE, so the answer is B ($67.5$).

Last month eight houses were sold in Greenvale.

Upper bound for outlier is $566\,000+82\,500=648\,500$.

$980\,000>648\,500$, hence the most expensive house sold is an outlier.

With the outlier present, median is $\$528\,000$ and mean is $\$583\,750$.

With the outlier removed, median is $\$528\,000$ and mean is $\$527\,143$ (to the nearest dollar).

525.stem:
The point $T$ is the peak of a mountain and the point $O$ is directly below the mountain's peak. The point $Y$ is due east of $O$ and the angle of elevation of $T$ from $Y$ is $60^\circ$. The point $F$ is 4 km south-west of $Y$. The points $O$, $Y$ and $F$ are on level ground. The angle of elevation of $T$ from $F$ is $45^\circ$.

\exfigure{1630_q29_1}

figures.cap: 3D diagram: mountain TO height h, Y east of O with elevation 60 deg, F 4 km from Y with elevation 45 deg; NOT TO SCALE
solution sketch: 30-60-90 triangle
solution sketch: triangle FOY with theta at F

parts.latex:
Let the height of the mountain be $h$.

Show that $OY=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the value of $h$, correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.latex: Find the bearing of point $O$ from point $F$, correct to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle TYO$, right-angled at $O$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{OY} \\ \therefore\ OY &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}} \end{aligned}$$
The exact value $\tan 60^\circ=\sqrt{3}$ comes from the $30^\circ$–$60^\circ$–$90^\circ$ triangle:

\exfigure{1630_q29_s1}

In $\triangle TFO$, $\angle TFO=45^\circ$, $\angle TOF=90^\circ$

$\therefore\ \angle OTF=45^\circ$

$\therefore\ \triangle TFO$ is isosceles and $OF=h$

In $\triangle FOY$, $\angle OYF=45^\circ$ ($F$ is south-west of $Y$ and $O$ is due west of $Y$). By the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} h^2 &= \left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+4^2-2\times 4\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\cos 45^\circ \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{h^2}{3}+16-\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}} \end{aligned}$$
$$\dfrac{2h^2}{3}+\dfrac{8h}{\sqrt{6}}-16=0$$
$$\begin{aligned} h &= \dfrac{-\frac{8}{\sqrt{6}}\pm\sqrt{\frac{64}{6}+4\times\frac{2}{3}\times 16}}{\frac{4}{3}} \\ &= 3.03 \quad\text{since } h>0 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds a quadratic expression in $h$, or equivalent merit
Attempts to use the cosine rule to find a value for $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{1630_q29_s2}

In $\triangle FOY$, let $\theta=\angle OFY$. By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\theta}{\frac{h}{\sqrt{3}}} &= \dfrac{\sin 45^\circ}{h} \\ \sin\theta &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}\sqrt{3}} \\ \theta &= 24.09\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 24^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$Y$ is on a bearing of $045^\circ$ from $F$, and $O$ is $\theta$ further anticlockwise:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 45^\circ-24^\circ \\ &\approx 021^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to find the bearing, or equivalent merit

539.stem:
The number of cars parked in a carpark is recorded each day for thirteen days. The dataset is listed in ascending order:

$$12,\ 15,\ 15,\ 17,\ 19,\ 20,\ 22,\ 24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 28,\ 30 \text{ and } m.$$

parts.latex: What is the interquartile range of this dataset?
parts.note: Interquartile range of a data set: Standard data analysis, not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-11-08

parts.latex: What is the greatest value of $m$ such that this dataset has no outlier?
parts.note: Outliers via Q3 + 1.5 IQR: Standard data analysis, not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-11-08

solutions.latex:
There are $13$ values, so the median is the 7th value, $22$.

The lower half is $12, 15, 15, 17, 19, 20$, so
$$Q_1=\dfrac{15+17}{2}=16$$
The upper half is $24, 25, 27, 28, 30, m$ (since $m\ge 30$), so
$$Q_3=\dfrac{27+28}{2}=27.5$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR}&=27.5-16\\ &=11.5 \end{aligned}$$

meta.check: Quartiles by the median-of-halves method (NESA convention); IQR does not depend on m since m is the 13th value.
meta.concern: Uses the HSC median-of-halves quartile method (median excluded); some calculators give the same 16 and 27.5 here.

solutions.latex:
An outlier is greater than $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$ (or less than $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$).
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}&=27.5+1.5\times 11.5\\ &=27.5+17.25\\ &=44.75 \end{aligned}$$
The lower bound is $16-17.25=-1.25$, so $12$ is not an outlier.

$m$ is a number of cars, so it is a whole number with $m\le 44.75$.

$\therefore$ the greatest value of $m$ is $44$.

meta.check: Fence computed twice; checked that m=44 gives no outlier and m=45 does (quartiles unchanged).
meta.concern: Answer 44 assumes m must be a whole number (count of cars); a marker may also accept 44.75 if m is not taken as an integer.

parts.latex:
Maya plans to go on an overseas trip in 5 years’ time. Maya expects that the trip will cost \$14 000. To save for the trip, Maya began by contributing \$750 every 6 months into an annuity. After making a number of payments, Maya realised that the annuity would not reach \$14 000 in 5 years. Maya decides to double the contribution until the trip.

The interest rate was $2\%$ per annum compounding half yearly.

\exfigure{1632_q27_1}

What is the maximum number of \$750 contributions Maya could make before she will need to double her payments to reach \$14 000?
parts.note: Annuity future-value interest-factor table look-up (owner ruling: tables moved to Standard).

solutions.latex:
Contributions are every 6 months for 5 years, so $n=5\times2=10$ periods, at $r=\dfrac{2\%}{2}=1\%=0.01$ per period.

If all $10$ contributions were $\$750$, the future value (table: rate $0.01$, period $10$) would be
$$750\times10.4622=\$7846.65$$
Doubling a contribution adds another $\$750$, so if the last $m$ contributions are doubled, the extra amount is $\$750$ times the future value of an annuity of $\$1$ for $m$ periods, $\text{FV}_m$. We need
$$\begin{aligned} 7846.65+750\times\text{FV}_m&\ge14\,000\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge\dfrac{14\,000-7846.65}{750}\\ \text{FV}_m&\ge8.2045\end{aligned}$$
From the table, $\text{FV}_8=8.2857\ge8.2045$, while $\text{FV}_7=\dfrac{1.01^7-1}{0.01}\approx7.2135<8.2045$.

So at least the last $8$ contributions must be doubled, leaving at most $10-8=2$ contributions of $\$750$.

Check: $750\times10.4622+750\times8.2857=\$14\,060.93\ge\$14\,000$.
$$\therefore\ \text{maximum number of } \$750 \text{ contributions}=2$$
criteria: Uses the table to find that at least $8$ contributions must be doubled, or equivalent merit
Forms a correct inequality or equation for the future value of the mixed contributions, or equivalent merit
Uses $r=0.01$ and $n=10$ with the table, or equivalent merit

557.stem:
A pyramid $MABCD$ has its vertex $M$ vertically above $O$, the centre of its square base $ABCD$, as shown. $AM=\ell$ cm and makes an angle of $\theta$ with the base.

\exfigure{1632_q30_1}

figures.cap: square-based pyramid MABCD with AM = l cm at angle theta to base

parts.latex:
Let $V$ be the volume of the pyramid.

Show that $V=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $\theta$, in radians, for which the volume of the pyramid is a maximum. Give your answer correct to 2 decimal places.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

solutions.latex:
In triangle $AOM$ (right angle at $O$, $\angle MAO=\theta$), using the sine and cosine ratios:
$$\begin{aligned} MO&=\ell\sin\theta\\ AO&=\ell\cos\theta\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is the centre of the square, so the diagonal $AC=2AO=2\ell\cos\theta$.

By Pythagoras' theorem, a square with side $s$ has $s^2+s^2=AC^2$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{base area}=s^2&=\dfrac{(2\ell\cos\theta)^2}{2}\\ &=2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
The volume of a pyramid is $\dfrac{1}{3}\times\text{base area}\times\text{height}$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\dfrac{1}{3}\times2\ell^2\cos^2\theta\times\ell\sin\theta\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\sin\theta\cos^2\theta\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the base area $2\ell^2\cos^2\theta$ and the height $\ell\sin\theta$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Checked with l=1, theta=pi/4: half-diagonal 0.7071, side 1, height 0.7071, V=0.2357 = (2/3)(0.7071)(0.5).

solutions.latex:
Here $\ell$ is constant and $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{d\theta}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=\cos^2\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-2\cos\theta\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{d\theta}&=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\left(\cos^3\theta-2\sin^2\theta\cos\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta\left(\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta\right)\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $\cos\theta\ne0$ when $0<\theta<\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so
$$\begin{aligned} \cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta&=0\\ \tan^2\theta&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ \tan\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2} &&(\tan\theta>0)\\ \theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\approx0.6155\end{aligned}$$
Nature: $\dfrac{2\ell^3}{3}\cos\theta>0$, so the sign of $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ is decided by
$$\cos^2\theta-2\sin^2\theta=\cos^2\theta\left(1-2\tan^2\theta\right)$$
that is, by $1-2\tan^2\theta$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta&=0.5: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx0.40>0 &&V \text{ increasing}\\ \theta&=0.7: &1-2\tan^2\theta&\approx-0.42<0 &&V \text{ decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the stationary point is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ \theta\approx0.62$$
criteria: Finds $\theta\approx0.62$ without justifying the maximum, or equivalent merit
Finds a correct factorised $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ and sets it equal to $0$, or equivalent merit
Finds $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta}$ using the product rule, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Grid search of sin t cos^2 t on (0, pi/2): max at 0.61548 = atan(1/sqrt2).

Using a calculator, with ice cream sales as the independent variable:

parts.latex: Find the bearing of $B$ from $C$ to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $TCA$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\tan 35^\circ=\dfrac{40}{AC}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ AC &= \dfrac{40}{\tan 35^\circ}\\ &= 57.1259\ldots\\ &= 57.13 \text{ metres} \quad (\text{2 decimal places})\end{aligned}$$

In right-angled triangle $TCB$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{40}{BC}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ BC &= \dfrac{40}{\tan 30^\circ}\\ &= 69.28 \text{ metres} \quad (\text{2 decimal places})\end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ACB$, with $AC=57.13$ from part (a) and $AB=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle ACB &= \dfrac{57.13^2+69.28^2-100^2}{2\times(57.13)\times(69.28)}\\ &= -0.24462\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \angle ACB=104^\circ \quad (\text{nearest degree})$$
$A$ is due east of $C$ (bearing $090^\circ$), so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing of } B \text{ from } C &= 104^\circ+90^\circ\\ &= 194^\circ\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the angle at $C$, or equivalent merit
Finds the length of $BC$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A vertical tower of height $h$ metres stands on horizontal ground. From a point $P$ on the ground due east of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $45^\circ$. From a point $Q$ on the ground due south of the tower the angle of elevation of the top of the tower is $30^\circ$. If the distance $PQ$ is 40 metres, find the exact height of the tower.

\exfigure{1359_q29_1}
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
Let $R$ be the base of the tower. In right-angled triangles $PRT$ and $QRT$, using the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 45^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \qquad \tan 30^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ 1 &= \dfrac{h}{PR} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} &= \dfrac{h}{QR} \\ PR &= h & QR &= \sqrt{3}h \end{aligned}$$
$P$ is due east and $Q$ due south of $R$, so $\angle PRQ = 90^\circ$. Using Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle PRQ$:
$$\begin{aligned} 40^2 &= h^2 + \left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2 \\ 1600 &= 4h^2 \\ h^2 &= 400 \\ h &= \pm 20 \end{aligned}$$
$h > 0$, so $h = 20$ m.
criteria: Three of: correct $PR$, correct $QR$, correct substitution into Pythagoras' theorem, correct answer, or equivalent merit
Two of the above, or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

901.stem:
The figure below shows three buoys at sea at $A$, $B$ and $C$. A helicopter flies along $FH$ and then $HG$, where $F$, $G$ and $H$ are three points of the same height vertically above $A$, $B$ and $C$, respectively. When the helicopter reaches $H$, the angles of depression of $A$ and $B$ from the helicopter are $60^{\circ}$ and $30^{\circ}$, respectively. The true bearings of $A$ and $B$ from $C$ are $250^{\circ}$ and $130^{\circ}$, respectively. The distance between $A$ and $B$ is $100\sqrt{13}$ km.

\exfigure{1362_q33_1}

figures.cap: 3D diagram: helicopter at H above C, angles of depression 60 and 30 degrees to A and B, AB = 100 sqrt13 km, AC = x km
solution sketch: sketch of the upward parabola in t, negative between its roots

parts.latex: Show that the distance between $A$ and C is $100$ km.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.latex:
At 9 a.m., two destroyers start travelling from $A$ and $B$ in the direction of $C$ and continue past $C$ in the same straight lines. The destroyer at $A$ travels along $AC$ with a uniform speed of $20$ km/h, while the destroyer at $B$ travels along $BC$ with a uniform speed of $50$ km/h.

Show that the distance between the two destroyers after travelling for $t$ hours is $10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}$.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

parts.latex:
The destroyers are known to be “on alert” when they are less than $40$ km apart.

During what times will the two destroyers be “on alert”?
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

solutions.latex:
Using the bearings from $C$:
$$\begin{aligned} \angle ACB&=250^{\circ}-130^{\circ}\\ &=120^{\circ} \end{aligned}$$
Let $AC=x$. In right-angled triangle $AHC$, the angle of depression gives $\angle HAC=60^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 60^{\circ}&=\dfrac{h}{x}\\ x&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^{\circ}}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\\ h&=\sqrt{3}x \end{aligned}$$
In right-angled triangle $BHC$, $\angle HBC=30^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 30^{\circ}&=\dfrac{h}{BC}\\ BC&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 30^{\circ}}=\dfrac{h}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}}=\sqrt{3}h\\ &=\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}x=3x \end{aligned}$$
Using the cosine rule in triangle $ABC$, $AB^2=AC^2+BC^2-2\times AC\times BC\times\cos 120^{\circ}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \left(100\sqrt{13}\right)^2&=\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2-2\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}h\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ 10\,000\times 13&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2+h^2\\ 130\,000&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+4h^2=\dfrac{13h^2}{3}\\ 13h^2&=3\times 130\,000\\ h^2&=3\times 10\,000\\ h&=\pm\sqrt{30\,000} \end{aligned}$$
$h>0$, so $h=\sqrt{30\,000}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ AC=x&=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{30\,000}}{\sqrt{3}}=\sqrt{10\,000}=100\text{ km}\\ BC&=\sqrt{3}h=\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{30\,000}=\sqrt{90\,000}=300\text{ km} \end{aligned}$$
Or, using $BC=3x$:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2&=x^2+(3x)^2-2\times x\times 3x\times\cos 120^{\circ}\\ \left(100\sqrt{13}\right)^2&=x^2+9x^2-6x^2\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ 10\,000\times 13&=10x^2+3x^2\\ 130\,000&=13x^2\\ x^2&=10\,000 \end{aligned}$$
$x>0$, so $x=100$, and $BC=3x=300$ km.
criteria: Uses the cosine rule correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds $AC$ and $BC$ in terms of $h$ (or $BC=3x$), or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: BC = 300 km (all distances are in km), not 300 m.

solutions.latex:
After $t$ hours the distances $AC$ and $BC$ are $100-20t$ and $300-50t$ respectively. The angle at $C$ is still $120^{\circ}$, so by the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} AB^2&=(100-20t)^2+(300-50t)^2-2(100-20t)(300-50t)\cos 120^{\circ}\\ &=10\,000-4000t+400t^2+90\,000-30\,000t+2500t^2-2\left(30\,000-5000t-6000t+1000t^2\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=130\,000-45\,000t+3900t^2\\ &=100\left(1300-450t+39t^2\right) \end{aligned}$$
$AB>0$, so
$$\begin{aligned} AB&=\sqrt{100\left(1300-450t+39t^2\right)}\\ &=10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes the correct distances after $t$ hours into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct distances after $t$ hours in the cosine rule
meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).
meta.marker_note: $100+20t$ and $300+50t$ were also accepted.

solutions.latex:
The destroyers are on alert when $AB<40$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}&<40\\ \sqrt{1300-450t+39t^2}&<4 &&(\text{divide by } 10)\\ 1300-450t+39t^2&<16 &&(\text{square})\\ 39t^2-450t+1284&<0 &&(\text{subtract } 16) \end{aligned}$$
Solving $39t^2-450t+1284=0$ with the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned} t&=\dfrac{450\pm\sqrt{450^2-4\times 39\times 1284}}{2\times 39}\\ &=\dfrac{450\pm\sqrt{2196}}{78}\\ &=\dfrac{75\pm\sqrt{61}}{13} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1362_q33_s1}

The parabola is concave up, so it is negative between its roots:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{450-\sqrt{450^2-4\times 39\times 1284}}{78}&<t<\dfrac{450+\sqrt{450^2-4\times 39\times 1284}}{78}\\ 5.168442333&<t<6.370019206 \end{aligned}$$
$$5\text{ h }10\text{ min }6.39\text{ s}<t<6\text{ h }22\text{ min }12.07\text{ s}$$
where $t$ is the time after 9 am.

$\therefore$ The destroyers are on alert between 2:10 pm and 3:22 pm.
criteria: Solves the quadratic inequality for $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Students needed to select only reasoning that supported Team B being more successful, and state that; not additional information, even if correct (e.g. Team B being slightly positively skewed or symmetrical). The question said to use summary statistics. Correct terminology was required (median, not med), and correct percentages needed to be quoted. The justification required correct context: scores given were match scores, so a percentage of scores must be in this context (e.g. Team B scored more than 27 goals in $50\%$ of matches). A higher interquartile range or larger range does not justify higher scores (consider a team with $Q_1=10$ and $Q_3=20$, or lowest and highest scores 8 and 23). parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $OAT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan 30^\circ&=\dfrac{OT}{18}\\ OT&=18\tan 30^\circ\\ &=\dfrac{18}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is due west of $A$ (bearing $270^\circ$) and $B$ is on a bearing of $210^\circ$ from $A$, so $\angle OAB=60^\circ$.

Applying the cosine rule in triangle $OAB$:
$$\begin{aligned}OB&=\sqrt{18^2+12^2-2(18)(12)\cos 60^\circ}\\ &=\sqrt{252}\end{aligned}$$
In right-angled triangle $OBT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\tan\theta&=\dfrac{OT}{OB}\\ \theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\frac{18}{\sqrt{3}}}{\sqrt{252}}\right)\\ &=33^\circ\ (\text{nearest degree})\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Calculates $OB$ correctly (exact form), or equivalent merit

993.stem:
A tall pole $OT$ is held in place vertically by ropes anchored by two pegs in the ground 10 metres apart at $A$ and $B$ as shown. $A$ is due west of $O$, and $B$ is at a bearing of $240^\circ\text{T}$ from $O$. The rope connecting the top of the pole $T$ to the peg at $A$ is $3\sqrt{3}$ metres long and makes an angle of $60^\circ$ with the ground.

\exfigure{1367_q24_1}

figures.cap: 3D diagram: vertical pole OT, pegs A (due west of O) and B on the ground, AB = 10 m, TA = 3√3 m at 60° to the ground, TB = ℓ, bearing 240° from O

parts.latex: Show that $OB=\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}$ metres.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.latex:
Hence or otherwise, find the length of the rope, $\ell$, connecting $T$ and $B$.

Give your answer to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $AOT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\cos 60^\circ&=\dfrac{AO}{3\sqrt{3}}\\ AO&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$A$ is due west of $O$ (bearing $270^\circ$) and $B$ is on a bearing of $240^\circ$ from $O$:
$$\angle AOB=270^\circ-240^\circ=30^\circ$$
Applying the cosine rule in triangle $AOB$:
$$\begin{aligned}10^2&=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)^2+(OB)^2-2\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)(OB)\cos 30^\circ\\ 100&=\dfrac{27}{4}+(OB)^2-3\sqrt{3}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}(OB)\\ (OB)^2-\dfrac{9}{2}(OB)-\dfrac{373}{4}&=0\\ 4(OB)^2-18(OB)-373&=0\end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula:
$$\begin{aligned}OB&=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{18^2-4\times 4\times(-373)}}{2\times 4}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm\sqrt{6292}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{18\pm 22\sqrt{13}}{8}\\ &=\dfrac{9\pm 11\sqrt{13}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Since $OB>0$:
$$OB=\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Forms a quadratic equation in $OB$, or equivalent merit
Applies the cosine rule to $\triangle OAB$, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct value of $AO$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In right-angled triangle $AOT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin 60^\circ&=\dfrac{OT}{3\sqrt{3}}\\ OT&=\dfrac{9}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Applying Pythagoras' theorem in right-angled triangle $BOT$:
$$\begin{aligned}\ell^2&=OB^2+OT^2\\ &=\left(\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right)^2\\ \ell&=\sqrt{\left(\dfrac{9+11\sqrt{13}}{4}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{9}{2}\right)^2}\quad(\ell>0)\\ &=12.97\ldots\\ &\approx 13\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $OT$, or equivalent merit

Spiro is borrowing \$30 000, to be repaid with monthly repayments over 5 years.

How much interest will be paid on the loan?

parts.latex: Calculate the percentage flat rate of interest per annum on this loan.
parts.note: Flat rate interest: in neither 2024 syllabus

solutions.latex:
From the table, the monthly repayment is \$683.

Total repayments over 5 years:
$$683\times12\times5=40\,980$$
Interest paid:
$$40\,980-30\,000=10\,980$$
$\therefore$ The interest paid on the loan is \$10 980.
criteria: Finds correct monthly repayment from table, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the flat-rate interest formula $I=Prn$ with $I=10\,980$, $P=30\,000$ and $n=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\,980&=30\,000\times r\times5\\ r&=10\,980\div30\,000\div5\\ &=0.0732\\ &=7.32\% \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The flat rate of interest is $7.32\%$ per annum.
criteria: Correct substitution into simple interest formula and attempts to solve for $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:

Steve suspects that the bivariate relationship between $x$ and $y$ is exponential. He decides to transform the data to make the relationship appear linear by finding the natural logarithm of the view times, and recording those values in the table shown.

By finding the equation of the least-squares regression line of the transformed data, predict the actual view time on the YouTube channel in the 7th year. Give your answer correct to the nearest hour.
parts.note: Least-squares regression on log-transformed data: bivariate data analysis (Standard), not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-12-S2-08

solutions.latex:
Using REG mode on the calculator with the transformed data, the least-squares regression line is
$$\ln(y)=1.124x+2.85$$
In the 7th year, $x=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln(y)&=1.124\times7+2.85\\ &=10.718 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$\begin{aligned} y&=e^{10.718}\\ &=45161.48948 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Steve predicts that the YouTube channel will achieve 45 161 hours of view time in the 7th year, correct to the nearest hour.
criteria: Correctly finds value for $\ln(y)$ in the 7th year, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A set of scores in a data set has a median of 72, an interquartile range of 14 and a variance of 4.

Each score has 3 added to it and each resulting score is then doubled to form a new set of scores.

What is the median, interquartile range, and variance of the new set of scores?
parts.note: Effect of linear changes on median, IQR and variance of a data set · Standard: MST-11-08

solutions.latex:
The median is a specific score, so it also has 3 added and is then doubled.

The interquartile range and variance are measures of spread, so they are unaffected by adding 3 to each score; doubling multiplies the IQR by 2 and the variance by $2^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Median}&=(72+3)\times 2\\ &=150 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR}&=14\times 2\\ &=28 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Variance}&=4\times 2^2\\ &=16 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The table below shows the future value of annuity with a contribution of \$1 at the end of each period.

\extable{1372_q33_t1}

Kevin opened an account and deposited \$15 000 at the end of each year for 6 years.

At the end of the 7th year, he deposited \$20 000 in the same account and continued to deposit \$20 000 at end of each year until the end of the 10th year.

He made no more deposits after the end of the 10th year.

The money in his account was earning interest at 2.5% per annum compounded annually.

How much money will Kevin have in his account at the end of 15 years?
parts.note: Annuity interest-factor table look-up is removed (annuities by GP formula only) · Standard: MST-12-S2-03

solutions.latex:
Using the 2.50% column of the table: the balance at the end of the first 6 years is the future value factor for 6 periods times the deposit of \$15 000:
$$6.38774\times\$15\,000=\$95\,816.10$$
This amount continues to earn interest for the remaining 9 years at 2.50% per annum, so it is multiplied by $1.025^9$.

Similarly, the four \$20 000 deposits (end of years 7 to 10) are worth $4.15252\times\$20\,000$ at the end of year 10, and earn interest for 5 more years:
$$4.15252\times\$20\,000\times1.025^5$$
Thus the final account balance at the end of 15 years is:
$$\begin{aligned}&6.38774\times\$15\,000\times1.025^9+4.15252\times\$20\,000\times1.025^5\\&=\$213\,625.08\text{ (nearest cent)}\end{aligned}$$
Alternate method (in stages, rounding to the nearest cent):
$$\begin{aligned}\text{End of 6 years: }&6.38774\times\$15\,000=\$95\,816.10\\\text{End of 10 years: }&4.15252\times\$20\,000+\$95\,816.10\times1.025^4=\$188\,813.45\\\text{End of 15 years: }&\$188\,813.45\times1.025^5=\$213\,625.09\end{aligned}$$
Depending on how the stages are rounded, the final result differs by a few cents.
criteria: Applies the interest rate in the years after deposits have stopped, or equivalent merit
Takes the appropriate products of deposit amount and future value, or equivalent merit
Identifies the appropriate values in the table, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the main method's final value $215 974.18 does not match its own expression, which evaluates to $213 625.08 (agreeing with the source's alternate method, $213 625.09).

parts.latex: Find $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to 0}\dfrac{4x-\tan 2x}{\sin 5x}$
parts.note: Trigonometric limits (lim sin x/x = 1) have no 2024 Advanced dot point

solutions.latex:
Splitting the limit and using $\displaystyle\lim_{\theta\to0}\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\theta}=\lim_{\theta\to0}\dfrac{\tan\theta}{\theta}=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{4x-\tan 2x}{\sin 5x}&=\lim_{x\to0}\left(\dfrac{4x}{\sin 5x}-\dfrac{\tan 2x}{\sin 5x}\right)\\&=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{4x}{\sin 5x}-\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\tan 2x}{\sin 5x}\\&=\lim_{x\to0}\left(\dfrac{5x}{\sin 5x}\times\dfrac{4}{5}\right)-\lim_{x\to0}\left(\dfrac{5x}{\sin 5x}\times\dfrac{1}{5x}\times\dfrac{\tan 2x}{2x}\times 2x\right)\\&=\dfrac{4}{5}-\dfrac{2}{5}\\&=\dfrac{2}{5}\end{aligned}$$

First 4 years: the table value at $3\%$ for 4 periods is $4.1836$:

parts.latex: Use the mean $\bar{y}=72$ of the \textit{Calculus} marks and the least squares regression line to find the mean $\bar{x}$ of the \textit{Functions} marks, and hence the missing \textit{Functions} mark for student H.

parts.latex: Another student in the same class sat the \textit{Functions} test but misses the \textit{Calculus} test. solutions.latex:
The least squares regression line passes through $(\bar{x},\bar{y})$, so substitute $y=\bar{y}=72$:
$$\begin{aligned}72&=0.72\bar{x}+18\\0.72\bar{x}&=54\\\bar{x}&=75\end{aligned}$$
Let $x$ be student H's mark. The mean of the eight marks is $75$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{63+59+69+83+77+75+85+x}{8}&=75\\511+x&=600\\x&=89\end{aligned}$$

Yes. $r=0.9$ indicates a strong positive correlation between the tests, so using the line would be justified statistically.

The limitations of the model could also be discussed: extrapolation would not be justified.

The median is higher inside, so the plants inside are taller.

parts.latex:
Consider the set of scores:

$$\mathbf{9\quad 17\quad 20\quad 23\quad 24\quad 27\quad 27\quad 28\quad 30\quad 31\quad 39\quad 47}$$

Which of the scores could be considered an outlier?
parts.note: Outliers via IQR of a data set · Standard: MST-11-08

solutions.latex:
$$Q_1=21.5,\quad Q_2=27,\quad Q_3=30.5$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{IQR} &= Q_3-Q_1 \\ &= 30.5-21.5 \\ &= 9 \end{aligned}$$

A score is an outlier if it is below $Q_1-1.5\times\text{IQR}$ or above $Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lower bound} &= 21.5-1.5\times 9 = 8 \\ \text{Upper bound} &= 30.5+1.5\times 9 = 44 \end{aligned}$$

Since $9>8$, the score $9$ is not an outlier, and $47>44$, so only $47$ is an outlier.

David is in a life raft, $D$, and Anna is in a cabin cruiser, $A$, searching for him.

They are in contact by mobile telephone. David tells Anna that he can see the top of the mountain Mt Hope, $H$.

From David's position, the mountain has a bearing of $340^\circ$ and the angle of elevation to the top of the mountain is $12^\circ$.

Anna can also see Mt Hope. From her position, the mountain has a bearing of $070^\circ$ and the top of the mountain has an angle of elevation of $19^\circ$. The top of Mt Hope is $1\,244$ m above sea level.

\exfigure{339_q33_1}

Find the distance of the life raft from Anna's position.

Give your answer correct to two decimal places.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{339_q33_s1}

Let $B$ be the point at sea level directly below $H$, so $HB=1244$ m.

In $\triangle ABH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle AHB=90^\circ-19^\circ=71^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s2}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 71^\circ &= \dfrac{AB}{1244} \\ AB &= 1244\tan 71^\circ \end{aligned}$$

In $\triangle BDH$, right-angled at $B$, $\angle BHD=90^\circ-12^\circ=78^\circ$:

\exfigure{339_q33_s3}

$$\begin{aligned} \tan 78^\circ &= \dfrac{BD}{1244} \\ BD &= 1244\tan 78^\circ \end{aligned}$$

The bearings of $B$ from $A$ ($070^\circ$) and from $D$ ($340^\circ$) differ by $70^\circ+20^\circ=90^\circ$, so $\angle ABD=90^\circ$.

By Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle ABD$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD^2 &= AB^2+BD^2 \\ &= (1244\tan 71^\circ)^2+(1244\tan 78^\circ)^2 \\ &= 47\,305\,057.68 \end{aligned}$$

Since $AD>0$:

$$\begin{aligned} AD &= \sqrt{47\,305\,057.68} \\ &= 6877.867\ldots \\ &\approx 6877.87\text{ m (2 decimal places)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes substantial progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit
Makes some progress towards the solution, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Read two points on the line of best fit from the graph: $(37,130)$ and $(55,166)$.
$$m=\dfrac{166-130}{55-37}=\dfrac{36}{18}=2$$
So the equation has the form $P=c+2A$.

Substitute $(37,130)$:
$$\begin{aligned}130&=c+2(37)\\c&=56\end{aligned}$$
Hence $P=56+2A$. The constant term is the value at $A=0$, which is well below the lowest data value of 130 at $A=37$, so $126$ and $130$ are not reasonable.

parts.note: Outliers via quartiles/IQR of a data set: Standard data analysis, not 2024 Advanced · Standard: MST-11-08

solutions.latex:
From the table, $Q_1=100$ and $Q_3=140$.
$$\text{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1=140-100=40$$
A score $x$ is an outlier if $x>Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}$:
$$\begin{aligned}Q_3+1.5\times\text{IQR}&=140+1.5\times40\\&=200\end{aligned}$$
Since $220>200$, 220 push ups is an outlier.

figures.cap: circle centre O on a vertical wall; A below O at height h, B on the circle with angle AOB = 90 degrees; D on the ground with elevations 30 and 60 degrees and angle ADB = 30 degrees (not to scale)

parts.latex: Write expressions for $AD$ and $BD$ in terms of $h$.
parts.note: Part of a 3D question: 3D trigonometry is Extension 1, not Advanced (owner 12 Nov)

parts.latex: Hence find the exact value of $h$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle with the angle of elevation $30^\circ$ at $D$ and height $h$ at $A$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin30^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{AD}\\AD&=\dfrac{h}{\sin30^\circ}=2h\end{aligned}$$
$O$ is $10$ m above $A$ and $OB$ is horizontal, so $B$ is $h+10$ m above the ground:
$$BD=\dfrac{h+10}{\sin60^\circ}=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$$
criteria: One correct expression, $AD=2h$ or $BD=\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle OAB$, $OA=OB=10$ and $\angle AOB=90^\circ$, so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$AB=\sqrt{10^2+10^2}=10\sqrt{2}$$
In $\triangle ABD$, use the cosine rule with $\angle ADB=30^\circ$:
$$\left(10\sqrt{2}\right)^2=\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+(2h)^2-2\left(\dfrac{2(h+10)}{\sqrt{3}}\right)(2h)\cos30^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned}200&=\dfrac{4h^2+80h+400}{3}+4h^2-4h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2+80h+400+12h^2-12h(h+10)\\600&=4h^2-40h+400\\0&=4h^2-40h-200\\&=4\left(h^2-10h-50\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$h=\dfrac{10\pm\sqrt{300}}{2}=5\pm5\sqrt{3}$$
Since $h>0$:
$$\therefore\ h=5+5\sqrt{3}\approx13.66$$
criteria: Correct quadratic equation in $h$, or equivalent merit
$AB=10\sqrt{2}$ and correct cosine rule equation, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: tower OH of height h; X due east of O with elevation 31 degrees; Y due south of X with elevation 25 degrees; XY = 150 m; right angles at O and X; north arrow

parts.latex: Show that $h=\dfrac{150\tan 25^\circ\tan 31^\circ}{\sqrt{\tan^2 31^\circ-\tan^2 25^\circ}}$.

parts.latex: Hence, find the height of the tower.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{373_q20_s1}

In the right-angled triangles with the tower of height $h$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan25^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{OY} &&\text{so } OY=\dfrac{h}{\tan25^\circ} \\ \tan31^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{OX} &&\text{so } OX=\dfrac{h}{\tan31^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
Pythagoras' theorem in triangle $OXY$:
$$\begin{aligned} 150^2+OX^2&=OY^2 \\ 150^2+\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan31^\circ}\right)^2&=\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan25^\circ}\right)^2 \\ 150^2+\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^231^\circ}&=\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^225^\circ} \\ h^2\left(\dfrac{1}{\tan^225^\circ}-\dfrac{1}{\tan^231^\circ}\right)&=150^2 \\ h^2\left(\dfrac{\tan^231^\circ-\tan^225^\circ}{\tan^225^\circ\tan^231^\circ}\right)&=150^2 \\ h^2&=\dfrac{150^2\tan^225^\circ\tan^231^\circ}{\tan^231^\circ-\tan^225^\circ} \\ h&=\dfrac{150\tan25^\circ\tan31^\circ}{\sqrt{\tan^231^\circ-\tan^225^\circ}} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Pythagoras in triangle $OXY$ with $OX$ and $OY$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit
$OX$ and $OY$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: regular octahedron ABCDE with centre O, edge 6 cm, M midpoint of BC, dashed AM and ME

parts.latex:
Two identical right pyramids with square bases and equilateral triangular faces are joined to form a regular octahedron.

The following diagram shows a regular octahedron with edge length 6 cm and centre at $O$. $AM$ and $ME$ are perpendicular heights of $\Delta ABC$ and $\Delta BCE$ respectively and point $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

\exfigure{382_q21_1}

Find the size of $\angle AME$, to the nearest degree.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
By symmetry $\triangle AMO\cong\triangle EMO$ (SSS: $AM=EM$, $AO=EO$, $MO$ common), so
$$\angle AME=2\times\angle AMO$$
In $\triangle AMC$ ($\angle AMC=90^\circ$, $AC=6$, $MC=3$), by Pythagoras' theorem:
$$\begin{aligned} AM &= \sqrt{6^2-3^2} \\ &= \sqrt{27} \\ &= 3\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
In $\triangle AMO$ (right angle at $O$, with $MO=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 6=3$, half the side of the square base):
$$\begin{aligned} \cos\angle AMO &= \dfrac{MO}{AM} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{3\sqrt{3}} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \\ \angle AMO &= \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \angle AME &= 2\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \\ &= 109.4712\ldots^\circ \\ &\approx 109^\circ \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Accept an alternative using the sine rule (finding $AM$ and $AE$, then the angle).

Rules 1,3,11,16,19,22.

figures.cap: scatterplot of Sales against Temperature in degrees C, rising then falling

parts.latex:
Mei owns a shop that sells smoothies (a type of cold drink). The scatterplot below shows the shop’s smoothie sales on 21 different days in 2024. The maximum temperature on each day is also shown.

\exfigure{369_q32_1}

Mei entered the data into a spreadsheet and calculated the following:

Pearson’s correlation coefficient: $r=0$

Least-squares regression line: $y=390$

Explain the meaning of the correlation coefficient and the least squares regression line with reference to Sales and Temperature.
parts.note: Bivariate data (correlation, least-squares regression line) has no 2024 Advanced dot point

solutions.latex:
The correlation coefficient $r=0$ indicates no linear correlation between Sales and Temperature.

This does not mean there is no relationship at all. The scatterplot shows a non-linear (possibly parabolic) trend: Sales increase as Temperature rises to about $25^\circ$C, then decrease. This is possibly because at cool temperatures there is less demand for smoothies, and at very high temperatures not many people are going out to the shop.

If the trend must be modelled by a straight line, $y=390$ is the best possible line. It is a horizontal line through the middle of the points, with about half of the points below the line and half above. The value $\$390$ represents the average Sales for a given day. A straight line cannot capture the 'increasing then decreasing' trend.
criteria: Two of the three points explained
One of the three points explained

meta.overwritten_from_source: Source said 'Temperature increases up to a certain point (25 degrees) then decreases'. It is Sales that increases then decreases as Temperature rises (checked on the scatterplot, peak near 25 degrees); now reads 'Sales increase as Temperature rises to about 25 degrees, then decrease'.
meta.marker_note: Saying 'no correlation' receives half a mark. Describing the non-linear trend receives half a mark (for example, Sales increases then decreases; Sales vs Temperature looks parabolic). Saying $y=390$ is the average value, or the centre of the points, receives half a mark.

parts.latex:
The future value of an annuity when \$1 is invested at the start of each period is shown in the table below.

\extable{402_q19_t1}

Jamie deposits \$800 into a savings account at the start of each month for 6 months. After the 6th deposit, Jamie stops making deposits but leaves the money in the savings account until exactly 12 months from the first deposit.

The interest rate on her savings account is 12% per annum, compounded monthly. What is the balance of Jamie’s savings account at the end of the 12 months?
parts.note: Annuity future value interest-factor TABLE look-up: 2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only

solutions.latex:
The table gives the future value of $\$1$ invested at the start of each period. Here the rate is $\dfrac{12\%}{12}=1\%$ per month and there are $6$ deposits, so the table factor is $6.2135$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{FV after 6 months}&=800\times6.2135\\ &=\$4970.80\end{aligned}$$
No more deposits are made, so this amount earns compound interest for a further $6$ months at $1\%$ per month, using $A=P(1+r)^n$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Balance}&=4970.80\times1.01^6\\ &\approx\$5276.60\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the balance after 12 months is }\$5276.60$$
criteria: Finds the FV correctly but incorrectly finds the final balance, OR fails to find the FV properly but correctly finds the final balance using the compound interest formula (carry error)

Read two points on the line from the graph: $(160,168)$ and $(170,175)$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{gradient}&=\dfrac{175-168}{170-160}=\dfrac{7}{10}\\ y-168&=\dfrac{7}{10}(x-160)\\ y&=\dfrac{7}{10}x+56\end{aligned}$$
In the variables of the graph, $d=\dfrac{7}{10}m+56$.

parts.latex: Ariel wants to have saved \$10 000 by the end of 8 years. She will make regular instalments at the end of each 6-month period into a bank account with $4\%$ interest p.a. compounded every 6 months. Find the value of each instalment that Ariel needs to make to reach her goal.

parts.note: Annuity future value interest-factor TABLE look-up: 2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only

solutions.latex:
Instalments are made every 6 months for 8 years: $16$ instalments, at $\dfrac{4}{2}=2\%$ per period. The table factor for $2\%$ and $16$ periods is $18.63929$.
$$\begin{aligned}10000&=18.63929\times m\\m&=\dfrac{10000}{18.63929}\\&=\$536.50\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses the table factor $18.63929$ ($2\%$, $16$ periods), or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric in the source was tick marks only; rows written by us. Checked: 10000/18.63929 = 536.50 and the factor equals the sum of 1.02^k, k=0..15.

solutions.latex:
After 2 years there have been $4$ instalments at $2\%$ per period, with table factor $4.12161$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=536.50\times 4.12161\\&=\$2211.24\end{aligned}$$

For the remaining 6 years there are $6\times 4=24$ quarters at $\dfrac{4}{4}=1\%$ per quarter. The balance after 2 years grows by compound interest, and the new instalments are an annuity with table factor $26.97346$.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=2211.24\times(1.01)^{24}+536.50\times 26.97346\\&=\$17278.95\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Excess}&=17278.95-10000\\&=\$7278.95\end{aligned}$$
So she has $\$7278.95$ more than her goal.
criteria: Obtains both terms of the total balance, or equivalent merit
Identifies $24$ periods at $1\%$, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: mast MT with pegs A (045 deg) and B (120 deg) and wires TA, TB
solution sketch: plan view from above: M, A and B with north, 100 m, 75 degree angle at M and area 10432 m^2

parts.latex: Find the distance between the base of the mast, $M$, and the peg at $B$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.latex:
Supporting wires are connected from each peg to the top of the mast at $T$.

By considering triangle $AMT$ and triangle $BMT$, find the height of the mast, given that the total length of the supporting wires is 380 m.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{515_q26_s1}

The bearings of $A$ and $B$ from $M$ are $045^\circ$ and $120^\circ$, so
$$\angle AMB=120^\circ-45^\circ=75^\circ$$
Let $MB=x$. Using the area formula $\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$ in triangle $AMB$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10\,432 &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times100\times x\times\sin75^\circ \\ x &= \dfrac{2\times10\,432}{100\sin75^\circ} \\ &\approx 216\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\angle AMB=75^\circ$ and substitutes into the area formula, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. \exfigure{515_q26_s1} kept (it was at the end of the source). Checked: x = 215.99999 m, i.e. 216 m.

solutions.latex:
The mast is vertical, so triangles $AMT$ and $BMT$ are right-angled at $M$. Let $MT=h$ and use Pythagoras' theorem with $MA=100$ and $MB=216$:
$$TA=\sqrt{h^2+100^2} \quad\text{and}\quad TB=\sqrt{h^2+216^2}$$
The total length of the wires is $380$ m.
$$\sqrt{h^2+100^2}+\sqrt{h^2+216^2}=380$$
Isolate one root and square both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} h^2+100^2+2\sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)}+h^2+216^2 &= 380^2 \\ 2\sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)} &= 380^2-216^2-100^2-2h^2 \\ &= 87\,744-2h^2 \\ \sqrt{(h^2+100^2)(h^2+216^2)} &= 43\,872-h^2 \end{aligned}$$
Square both sides again and let $u=h^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} (u+100^2)(u+216^2) &= (43\,872-u)^2 \\ u^2+100^2u+216^2u+100^2\times216^2 &= 43\,872^2-87\,744u+u^2 \\ 100^2u+216^2u+87\,744u &= 43\,872^2-100^2\times216^2 \\ 144\,400u &= 1\,458\,192\,384 \\ u &\approx 10\,098.285 \\ h &= \sqrt{10\,098.285} \\ &\approx 100.49\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms an equation in $h$ alone and reduces it to $u=h^2$ (or equivalent), or equivalent merit
Finds $TA$ and $TB$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. Checked: h = 100.49 m (TA = 141.77, TB = 238.23, sum 380.00). Squaring twice can introduce false roots; here h = 100.49 satisfies the original equation.

figures.cap: solution sketch: diagram of surveyors and tree

parts.latex:
Two surveyors, $A$ and $B$, stand on level ground to observe a large tree. The tree is directly north of surveyor $A$ who sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $52^\circ$.

Surveyor $B$ is 27 metres away from Surveyor $A$ on a bearing of $043^\circ$ and sights the top of the tree at an angle of elevation of $46^\circ$.

Find the height, $h$, of the tree correct to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tree seen from two points on level ground, elevation and bearings) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{833_q29_s1}

Let $C$ be the point at the base of the tree. Using the tangent ratio in the two right-angled triangles,
$$AC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}, \qquad BC = \dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}$$
In $\triangle ABC$, $AB = 27$ and $\angle CAB = 43^\circ$ (the bearing of $B$ from $A$ is $043^\circ$ and $C$ is due north of $A$). Apply the cosine rule.
$$\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 46^\circ}\right)^2 = \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\right)^2 + 27^2 - 2\times\dfrac{h}{\tan 52^\circ}\times 27\times\cos 43^\circ$$
Rearranging,
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \left(\dfrac{1}{\tan^2 52^\circ} - \dfrac{1}{\tan^2 46^\circ}\right)h^2 - \dfrac{54\cos 43^\circ}{\tan 52^\circ}h + 27^2 \\ 0 &\approx -0.32215h^2 - 30.85539h + 729 \end{aligned}$$
Using the quadratic formula, with $h > 0$,
$$h = \dfrac{30.855\ldots - \sqrt{30.855\ldots^2 - 4\times(-0.322\ldots)\times 729}}{2\times(-0.322\ldots)} \approx 19.6$$
$$\therefore h \approx 20 \text{ metres (to the nearest metre)}$$
criteria: Makes progress in solving for $h$, or equivalent merit
Forms a relationship, in terms of $h$, between the edges in the base triangle, or equivalent merit
Expresses the edge $AC$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Quadratic formula root choice: the negative-denominator form gives the positive root.

The four scores sum to $381$, so

Anthony stands at point A, 230 m due east of the tower OT, of height $h$ metres. The angle of elevation of T from A is $15^\circ$. Brian, at point B, is due south of the tower OT. The angle of elevation to the top of the tower from B is $10^\circ$.

figures.cap: tower OT with points A (east) and B (south), angles 15 and 10 degrees

parts.latex: Show that the height of the tower is 61.6 metres correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (a tower seen from two points) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

parts.note: 3D trigonometry (a tower seen from two points) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

parts.latex: What is the bearing of Brian from Anthony?
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (a tower seen from two points) is now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle $OAT$, the angle at $A$ is $15^\circ$, the side opposite is $h$ and the adjacent side is $OA=230$.

Using $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 15^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{230} \\ h&=230\tan 15^\circ \\ &=61.6283\ldots \\ &=61.6 \text{ m (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$

In the right-angled triangle $OBT$, the angle at $B$ is $10^\circ$, the side opposite is $h$ and the adjacent side is $OB$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 10^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{OB} \\ OB&=\dfrac{61.6}{\tan 10^\circ} \\ &=349.3509\ldots \\ &=349 \text{ m (3 s.f.)} \end{aligned}$$
This is $350$ m if the exact part (i) answer is used.

Let $\angle OAB=\theta$, where $OB=349$ m (from part (ii)) and $OA=230$ m, in the right-angled triangle $OAB$.
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{349}{230}$$
so $\theta=56.614\ldots^\circ$.

Anthony is due east of $O$, so the bearing of $O$ from $A$ is $270^\circ$. Brian is south of $O$, so $B$ is to the south-west of $A$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Bearing} &= 270-56.614\ldots \\ &= 213.38\ldots \\ &\approx 213^\circ \text{ (nearest degree)} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing of Brian from Anthony is } 213^\circ$$

The most frequent scores are the lowest ones, $4$ and $5$, and the dots thin out steadily towards the higher scores, up to $10$.

So the tail of the distribution is on the right (the high values).

parts.note: Annuity interest-factor table look-up; 2024 Advanced annuities use the GP formula only.

solutions.latex:
For a $6$-period annuity, the number of periods is $3\times 2=6$ and the rate per period is $8\%\div 2=4\%$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= 3\times 2 \\ &= 6 \text{ half-years} \\ \text{Rate} &= 8\%\div 2 \\ &= 4\% \text{ per half-year} \\ \text{Future value} &= 700\times 6.6330 \\ &= \$4643.10 \end{aligned}$$

The table factor for $6$ periods at $4\%$ is $6.6330$.

meta.format_note: Source said '6 months' for the number of periods; the periods are half-years, so wording corrected.

solutions.latex:
Grace needs a future value of $\$6000$, with the same table factor $6.6330$.

$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= x\times 6.6330 \\ x &= \$904.57 \end{aligned}$$

The extra contribution needed is

$$\begin{aligned} \$904.57-\$700 &= \$204.57 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{Grace must contribute } \$204.57 \text{ more each half-year.}$$

meta.format_note: Source wrote 'Angela needs' for the extra amount; the question asks about Grace, so wording corrected.

parts.note: Outliers using IQR are not in 2024 Advanced; they are now Standard content.

solutions.latex:
The interquartile range is
$$\begin{aligned} IQR &= Q_3 - Q_1 \\ &= 16 - 10 \\ &= 6 \end{aligned}$$
The lower bound for outliers is
$$\begin{aligned} Q_1 - 1.5\times IQR &= 10 - 1.5\times 6 \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
The upper bound for outliers is
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 + 1.5\times IQR &= 16 + 1.5\times 6 \\ &= 25 \end{aligned}$$
The maximum range is the upper bound minus the lower bound.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Range} &= 25 - 1 \\ &= 24 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Significant progress towards correct solution, or equivalent merit

New mean:

solutions.latex:
The number of repayments is $4\times12=48$, and the monthly rate is
$$9\%\div12=0.75\%=0.0075$$
The present value of the loan equals the repayment times the table factor (48 periods, $0.75\%$):
$$22000=M\times40.18478$$
$$\begin{aligned} M&=\dfrac{22000}{40.18478} \\ &=547.4709\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Mark will repay } \$547.47 \text{ per month.}$$

The total repaid is
$$\begin{aligned} \$547.47\times48&=\$26\,278.56 \end{aligned}$$
The interest is the total repaid less the amount borrowed:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Interest}&=\$26\,278.56-\$22\,000 \\ &=\$4278.56 \end{aligned}$$
Note: using the unrounded repayment, $48\times\dfrac{22000}{40.18478}-22000=\$4278.61$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Interest}=\$4278.56$$

A hiker starts from point $P$ and walks 100 metres along a straight path to the north-east, arriving at point $Q$. A peak is located at point $R$, which is directly above point $X$. figures.cap: 3D diagram of hiker path PQ, peak R above X with angles of elevation 10 and 5 degrees

parts.latex: Show that $XP = h\cot 10^\circ$ and find a similar expression for $XQ$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (peak above level ground seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1

parts.latex: Hence, find the value of $h$. Give your answer correct to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (peak above level ground seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1

solutions.latex:
$\triangle RPX$ is right-angled at $X$, so by the tangent ratio:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 10^\circ &= \dfrac{RX}{XP} = \dfrac{h}{XP} \\ XP &= \dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ} \\ &= h\cot 10^\circ \end{aligned}$$
$\triangle RQX$ is right-angled at $X$, so similarly:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 5^\circ &= \dfrac{h}{XQ} \\ XQ &= h\cot 5^\circ \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows that $XP = h\cot 10^\circ$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using Pythagoras' theorem in $\triangle XPQ$:
$$\begin{aligned} XP^2 + PQ^2 &= XQ^2 \\ (h\cot 10^\circ)^2 + 100^2 &= (h\cot 5^\circ)^2 \\ h^2\cot^2 10^\circ + 10\,000 &= h^2\cot^2 5^\circ \\ 10\,000 &= h^2\left(\cot^2 5^\circ - \cot^2 10^\circ\right) \\ h^2 &= \dfrac{10\,000}{\cot^2 5^\circ - \cot^2 10^\circ} \\ h &= \sqrt{\dfrac{10\,000}{\cot^2 5^\circ - \cot^2 10^\circ}} \\ &= 10 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h = 10 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Makes $h^2$ the subject, or equivalent merit
Applies Pythagoras' theorem to $\triangle XPQ$, or equivalent merit

$$XP^2 + PQ^2 = XQ^2$$
Substituting $XP = h\cot 10^\circ$ and $XQ = h\cot 5^\circ$:
$$\begin{aligned} h^2\cot^2 10^\circ + 10\,000 &= h^2\cot^2 5^\circ \\ 10\,000 &= h^2\left(\cot^2 5^\circ - \cot^2 10^\circ\right) \\ h &= \sqrt{\dfrac{10\,000}{\cot^2 5^\circ - \cot^2 10^\circ}} \\ &\approx 10 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h \approx 10 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Makes $h^2$ the subject, or equivalent merit
Applies Pythagoras' theorem to $\triangle XPQ$, or equivalent merit

A footpath on horizontal ground has two parallel edges. $CD$ is a vertical street sign pole of height $h$ metres which stands with its base $C$ on one edge of the footpath. $A$ and $B$ are two points on the other edge of the footpath such that $AB=7$ m and $\angle ACB=60^\circ$. From $A$ and $B$, the angles of elevation to the top of the pole at $D$ are $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ respectively.

\exfigure{1334_q18_1}

figures.cap: pole CD of height h at C on one footpath edge; A, B on the other edge, AB = 7 m, width w, angles 60, 30, 60

parts.latex: Show that the exact height of the flagpole is $h=\sqrt{21}$ metres.

parts.latex: By considering the area of $\triangle ABC$, find the exact width $w$ of the footpath.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry question (whole question removed): now Year 11 Extension 1, not Advanced.

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle BCD$, using $\tan 60^\circ=\dfrac{h}{CB}$:
$$CB=\dfrac{h}{\tan 60^\circ}=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}$$
In $\triangle ACD$, using $\tan 30^\circ=\dfrac{h}{CA}$:
$$CA=\dfrac{h}{\tan30^\circ}=\sqrt{3}h$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle ABC$:
$$AB^2=CB^2+CA^2-2(CB)(CA)\cos 60^\circ$$
$$\begin{aligned}7^2&=\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^2+\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)^2-2\left(\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\sqrt{3}h\right)\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\49&=\dfrac{h^2}{3}+3h^2-h^2\\147&=7h^2\\h^2&=21\end{aligned}$$
Since $h>0$, $h=\sqrt{21}$ metres.
criteria: Substitutes into the cosine rule, or equivalent merit
Finds $CB$ and $CA$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Use the area formula with the angle at $C$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\triangle ABC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}(CB)(CA)\sin C\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{3}}\times\sqrt{3}h\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}h^2\\&=\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\times21\\&=\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Also, with base $AB=7$ and height $w$:
$$\begin{aligned}A_{\triangle ABC}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times7\times w\\\dfrac{21\sqrt{3}}{4}&=\dfrac{7w}{2}\\w&=\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the width of the footpath is } \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{ metres}$$
criteria: Equates the area with $\dfrac{1}{2}\times7\times w$, or equivalent merit
Finds the area using $\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin C$, or equivalent merit

parts.note: Outliers (quartiles/IQR) of a data set are not in 2024 Advanced; they are Mathematics Standard content.

solutions.latex:
There are $30$ scores. The cumulative frequencies are $10, 16, 28, 29, 29, 29, 30$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Median} &= 15.5\text{th score} = 120 \\ Q_1 &= 8\text{th score} = 100 \\ Q_3 &= 23\text{rd score} = 140 \\ IQR &= 140-100 = 40 \end{aligned}$$
A value is an outlier if it is above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3+1.5\times IQR &= 140+1.5\times40 \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$
Since $220>200$, $220$ push ups is an outlier.

Each sloping face makes $50^\circ$ with the horizontal. Half the width of the base is $3.5$ m.

In the right-angled triangle formed by the roof height $h_R$ and a horizontal run of $3.5$ m:
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{3.5}, \quad\text{so}\quad h_R = 3.5\tan 50^\circ$$
The slant height $h_\triangle$ of the sloping face satisfies
$$\begin{aligned} \sin 50^\circ &= \dfrac{h_R}{h_\triangle} \\ h_\triangle &= \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{\sin 50^\circ} \\ &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
The horizontal run $x$ on the end faces satisfies
$$\tan 50^\circ = \dfrac{h_R}{x} = \dfrac{3.5\tan 50^\circ}{x}, \quad\text{so}\quad x = 3.5$$
Then $EF = 10 - 2\times 3.5 = 3$ m.

The two triangular end faces have base $7$ and slant height $\dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}$. The two trapezium faces have parallel sides $3$ and $10$ and the same slant height.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{3.5}{\cos 50^\circ}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2 \times 7 + \dfrac{1}{2}(3 + 10)\times 2\right) \\ &\approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total area} \approx 108.9 \text{ m}^2 \text{ (1 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Correct expression for the total area, or equivalent merit
Finds the slant height and $EF$, or equivalent merit
Finds the slant height or the roof height, or equivalent merit
Sets up a correct trigonometric ratio, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source had no rubric; written by us. Source labels the trapezium slant height $h_\triangle$ in the first line, and I left that line out as it duplicates the later slant-height line; values checked: $3.5/\cos 50^\circ \times 20 \approx 108.9$.

solutions.latex:
$r=0.9$ is close to $1$ and positive.
$$\therefore\ \text{strong positive correlation}$$

Using the points $(2.5,1)$ and $(4.5,3.5)$ on the line, the gradient is
$$m=\dfrac{3.5-1}{4.5-2.5}=1.25$$
Using $y-y_1=m(x-x_1)$ with $(2.5,1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y-1&=1.25(x-2.5)\\ y&=1.25x-2.125\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y=1.25x-2.125$$
criteria: Finds the gradient using two points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $x=3$ (\$3000 is 3 thousand dollars) into the regression line.
$$\begin{aligned} y&=1.25\times3-2.125\\ &=1.625\end{aligned}$$
Since $y$ is in hundreds of thousands, this is about $162\,500$ visitors.
$$\therefore\ 162\,500 \text{ visitors}$$

$x=1.5$ lies outside the range of the data, so predicting there is extrapolation and is unreliable.

Alternatively, when $x=1.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=1.25(1.5)-2.125\\ &=-0.25\end{aligned}$$
This is negative, which makes no sense as the number of visitors cannot be negative.

3777.stem: Alice, Brett and Chris are all going to see the Eiffel Tower. Alice is due north of the tower, Chris is due east and Brett is on the line of sight between them. The angles of elevation to the top of the tower from Alice, Brett and Chris are $23^\circ$, $25^\circ$ and $32^\circ$ respectively.

parts.latex:
Show that the angle between the Eiffel Tower, Alice and Chris is represented by

$$\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ}$$
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

parts.latex: What is the bearing of Brett from the Eiffel Tower?
parts.note: 3D trigonometry: now Year 11 Extension 1 (2024 syllabus), not Advanced

solutions.latex:
Let $D$ be the base of the tower, $E$ its top and $h=DE$. Let $\theta=\angle DAC$, the angle between the tower, Alice and Chris. Since Alice is due north and Chris due east of the tower, $\angle ADC=90^\circ$.

In right-angled triangle $CDE$:
$$h=CD\tan 32^\circ,\quad\text{so } CD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 32^\circ}$$
In right-angled triangle $ADE$:
$$h=AD\tan 23^\circ,\quad\text{so } AD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}$$
In right-angled triangle $ADC$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan\theta&=\dfrac{CD}{AD}\\ &=\dfrac{h}{\tan 32^\circ}\div\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}\\ &=\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{\tan 23^\circ}{\tan 32^\circ}\approx 34.2^\circ$$
criteria: Expresses $CD$ and $AD$ in terms of $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source opening had an unfinished phrase ('and $\angle DAE$...'); removed it. Diagram for the solution (key 1036_q24_s1) is not added here.

solutions.latex:
In triangle $ADB$ (right-angled at the elevation triangles): $AD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 23^\circ}$ and $BD=\dfrac{h}{\tan 25^\circ}$. Also $\angle DAB=\theta\approx 34.2^\circ$, with $\angle ABD=\alpha$ and $\angle ADB=\beta$.

By the sine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\sin\alpha}{AD}&=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{BD}\\ \sin\alpha&=\sin\theta\times\dfrac{\tan 25^\circ}{\tan 23^\circ}\\ &\approx 0.61729 \end{aligned}$$
So $\alpha\approx 38^\circ$ or $\alpha\approx 142^\circ$ (ambiguous case).

If $\alpha=38^\circ$:
$$\beta=180^\circ-38^\circ-34^\circ=108^\circ$$
This is not valid, because $B$ lies between $A$ and $C$ so $0<\beta<90^\circ$.

Therefore $\alpha=142^\circ$, and
$$\beta=180^\circ-34^\circ-142^\circ\approx 4^\circ$$
Brett is $4^\circ$ east of north from the tower.
$$\therefore\ \text{the bearing is about } 004^\circ\text{T}$$
criteria: Rejects the ambiguous case, or equivalent merit
Applies the sine rule to find $\sin\alpha$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source opening phrase 'right-angled at the elevation triangles' tidied; a solution diagram (key 1036_q24_s1) would help but is not drawn here.

From the table, the future value of a \$1 annuity for 8 quarters at 3% per quarter is \$8.8923.

Let each quarterly instalment be $\$a$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8.8923\times a &= 5000 \\ a &= 5000\div 8.8923 \\ &\approx 562.28 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{each instalment is } \$562.28 \text{ quarterly}$$
criteria: Selects the correct table value, or correct procedure with an error in the table value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
After 1 year there are 4 quarters, so the table value at 3% for 4 periods is $4.1836$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Amount} &= 4.1836\times\$562.28 \\ &\approx \$2352.35 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Selects the correct table value, or equivalent merit

options.label: A

figures.cap: back-to-back stem and leaf plot, Table A and Table B

parts.note: Outliers from a stem-and-leaf plot (quartiles/IQR) are Standard content, not 2024 Advanced

solutions.latex:
An outlier lies above $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

Table A: $Q_1=14$, $Q_2=27$, $Q_3=35$.
$$\begin{aligned} IQR&=35-14=21\\ Q_3+1.5\times IQR&=35+1.5\times 21=66.5 \end{aligned}$$
Since $69>66.5$, 69 is an outlier for Table A.

Table B: $Q_1=17$, $Q_2=24$, $Q_3=45$.
$$\begin{aligned} IQR&=45-17=28\\ Q_3+1.5\times IQR&=45+1.5\times 28=87 \end{aligned}$$
Since $69<87$, 69 is not an outlier for Table B.

So 69 is an outlier for Table A only, and the correct option is B.

parts.latex:
Harrison wants to reduce his withdrawal to \$20 000 per year for the next 10 years, starting 5 years after his retirement.

If the amount he deposited when he opened the account was \$340 000, would he be able to make these planned withdrawals over the ten years? (Justify your answer with calculations)
parts.note: Annuity present value interest factor table look-up (2024 Advanced uses the GP formula only)

solutions.latex:
The present value of an annuity is the withdrawal times the factor from the table, using $r=0.02$ and $N=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Present value}&=\$36\,000\times4.7135\\&=\$169\,686\end{aligned}$$

The ten years of withdrawals start after year 5, so take the $\$20\,000$ annuity for 15 years and subtract the $\$20\,000$ annuity for 5 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Present value}&=20\,000\times12.8493-20\,000\times4.7135\\&=\$162\,716\end{aligned}$$
The total required is this plus the $\$169\,686$ from part (a).
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total}&=\$162\,716+\$169\,686\\&=\$332\,402\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \$340\,000 \text{ would be enough}$$
criteria: Working towards the correct amount for the ten year period, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: scatterplot of crop size against shrub height with regression line

parts.latex:
The gradient of the least-squares regression line can be found using the formula:

$$\text{gradient}=r\times\dfrac{\text{standard deviation of }y\text{ scores}}{\text{standard deviation of }x\text{ scores}}=r\dfrac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}.$$

Given that the least-squares regression line crosses the vertical axis at 0.339, find the equation of the regression line and hence predict the crop (in kg) from a 100 cm high shrub.
parts.note: Least-squares regression line and prediction from bivariate data are removed from Advanced (Standard content)

parts.latex: Use the statistical measures and the graph to justify the reliability of making predictions such as that in part (a) and determine the range of heights for which such predictions would continue to be reliable.
parts.note: Reliability of regression predictions (correlation, interpolation) is removed from Advanced (Standard content)

solutions.latex:
Use the given gradient formula with the statistics from the table.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{gradient}&=r\dfrac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}\\&=0.874\times\dfrac{0.61}{35.42}\\&=0.01505195\end{aligned}$$
The intercept is 0.339, so the equation is
$$y=0.01505195x+0.339$$
When $x=100$:
$$\begin{aligned}y&=0.01505195\times100+0.339\\&=1.844195\\&\approx1.84\text{ kg}\end{aligned}$$
(accept 1.85 kg from the graph)
criteria: Either the equation or the estimate correct, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The value $r=0.874$ shows a strong positive correlation between the variables, so predictions such as that in part (a) would be very reliable.

From the data, shrubs only begin producing berries from about 30 cm in height, and the mature shrubs are no taller than about 150 cm, as neither appears in the data.

Predictions would therefore only be reliable between about $x=30$ and $x=150$.
criteria: Either of these outlined clearly, or equivalent merit

Interest is $2\%$ per half-year and there are 4 half-years. From the table, the factor is $4.1216$.

parts.note: Describing association in bivariate data is Standard content, not 2024 Advanced.

criteria: Finds the rise or the run, or shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The line has the form $y=mx+c$, so
$$\text{Income}=0.8\times\text{Age}+c$$
The line of best fit passes through $(65,65)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 65 &= 0.8\times 65+c \\ c &= 13 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Income}=0.8\times\text{Age}+13$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Income} &= 0.8\times\text{Age}+13 \\ &= 0.8\times 80+13 \\ &= 77 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the income of an 80 year old person is } \$77\,000$$
People over the age of 65 often have a reduced income due to retirement, so the prediction in part (c) is not accurate.
The association is linear, positive and weak.

3951.stem:
A surveyor who is $y$ metres due south of a tower sees the top of it with an angle of elevation $8^\circ$.

A second surveyor is $x$ metres due east of the tower.

From her position the angle of elevation is $10^\circ$ to the top of the tower.

The two surveyors are 940 m apart.

\exfigure{156_q11g_1}

figures.cap: tower of height h, surveyors S (south, distance y, angle 8 degrees) and E (east, distance x, angle 10 degrees), SE = 940 m

parts.latex: Show that $y = \dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (two surveyors and a tower): now Year 11 Extension 1.

parts.latex: Find the height ($h$) of the tower to the nearest metre.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (two surveyors and a tower): now Year 11 Extension 1.

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle formed by the tower (height $h$), the base and the surveyor, the angle of elevation is $8^\circ$.
$$\begin{aligned} \tan 8^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{y}\\ y&=\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\end{aligned}$$

Similarly, for the second surveyor, $x=\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}$.

The surveyors and the base of the tower form a right-angled triangle (right angle at the base), so by Pythagoras' theorem
$$x^2+y^2=940^2$$
Substitute.
$$\begin{aligned} \left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 8^\circ}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{h}{\tan 10^\circ}\right)^2&=940^2\\ h^2\left(\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ\right)&=940^2\\ h&=\sqrt{\dfrac{940^2}{\cot^28^\circ+\cot^210^\circ}}\\ &\approx 103.3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The height of the tower is $103$ m, to the nearest metre.
criteria: Correct expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Which statement is true for an ungrouped data set with no outliers?
parts.note: Interquartile range and outliers of a data set are removed from 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

solutions.latex:
A value is an outlier if it lies more than $1.5\times IQR$ below $Q_1$ or above $Q_3$.

With no outliers, the smallest and largest scores lie within these fences, so the range is greatest when the data extend to the fences.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{largest range} &= (Q_3+1.5\,IQR)-(Q_1-1.5\,IQR) \\ &= (Q_3-Q_1)+3\,IQR \\ &= IQR+3\,IQR \\ &= 4\,IQR \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option C.

4025.stem:
Jasper records the number of Year 12 students who studied for at least one hour each day for each of the past ten days, the results were as follows:

15, 18, 20, 20, 22, 26, 28, 32, 34, 47

parts.latex: Find the mean correct to one decimal place.
parts.note: Mean of a raw data set (summary statistics) has no 2024 Advanced dot point.

parts.latex: Find the interquartile range.
parts.note: Interquartile range of a data set is removed from 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

parts.latex: Is 47 an outlier for this set of data? Justify your answer with calculations.
parts.note: Outliers (1.5 x IQR test) are removed from 2024 Advanced (Standard content).

solutions.latex:
The mean is the sum of the scores divided by the number of scores.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Mean} &= \dfrac{262}{10} \\ &= 26.2 \end{aligned}$$

The interquartile range is $Q_3 - Q_1$.
$$\begin{aligned} Q_3 - Q_1 &= 32 - 20 \\ &= 12 \end{aligned}$$

An outlier lies above the upper fence $Q_3 + 1.5 \times \text{IQR}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Upper fence} &= 32 + 1.5 \times 12 \\ &= 50 \end{aligned}$$
Since $47 < 50$, 47 is not an outlier.

parts.latex: A school has two History classes that sit an exam. Andy's class has 16 students and has a mean mark of 65%, whilst Juliana's class has 24 students. The combined mean for the 2 classes is 68.6%. Find the mean for the Juliana's class.
parts.note: Mean of a data set (combined means) has no 2024 Advanced dot point.

solutions.latex:
The combined total of marks equals the sum of the class totals. Let $x$ be the mean of Juliana's class.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{16\times 65 + 24x}{40} &= 68.6 \\ 1040 + 24x &= 2744 \\ 24x &= 1704 \\ x &= 71 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the mean of Juliana's class is } 71\%$$

parts.latex: Hence, or otherwise, find the angle of inclination from point $D$ to the peak of the mountain. Give your answer to the nearest minute.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (angle of elevation to a peak from two points on a plane): now Year 11 Extension 1.

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle ABD$:
$$\angle ABD=180^\circ-15^\circ-135^\circ=30^\circ$$
By the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$:
$$\dfrac{AB}{\sin135^\circ}=\dfrac{3.5}{\sin30^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned}AB&=\dfrac{3.5\sin135^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}\\&\approx4.950\text{ km}\ (3\text{ d.p.})\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Adequate working must be shown.
meta.format_note: Sketch/diagram of triangle $ABD$ and the vertical triangle $ABC$ could be added as a solution diagram (key 1309_q17_s1).

solutions.latex:
In the right-angled triangle $ABC$ (angle of inclination $36^\circ$ at $A$):
$$\tan36^\circ=\dfrac{CB}{AB}$$
$$\begin{aligned}CB&=AB\tan36^\circ\\&\approx4.950\times\tan36^\circ\\&\approx3.596\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
By the sine rule in $\triangle ABD$:
$$\dfrac{BD}{\sin15^\circ}=\dfrac{3.5}{\sin30^\circ}$$
$$\begin{aligned}BD&=\dfrac{3.5\sin15^\circ}{\sin30^\circ}\\&\approx1.812\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
In the right-angled triangle $CBD$:
$$\tan\angle CDB=\dfrac{CB}{BD}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\angle CDB&=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{3.596}{1.812}\right)\\&\approx63^\circ16'\ \text{(nearest minute)}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $CB$ or states $\theta=\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{CB}{BD}\right)$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: No penalty for rounding.

Charlie is applying for membership at a new golf club that has a strong reputation. The scores of his current club have a lower quartile of 110 and an upper quartile of 118 and Charlie’s score is not an outlier.

Given that the club he plans to join has scores with a lower quartile of 90 and an upper quartile of 106, can you assure Charlie that his score will not be an outlier in his new club? Justify your answer with appropriate calculations.
parts.note: Quartiles, IQR and outliers are not in 2024 Advanced (Mathematics Standard).

solutions.latex:
A score is an outlier if it lies outside $Q_1-1.5\times IQR$ and $Q_3+1.5\times IQR$.

Current club:
$$IQR=118-110=8$$
$$1.5\times IQR=12$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=118+12=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=110-12=98$$
$\therefore$ Charlie's score is between $98$ and $130$.

New club:
$$IQR=106-90=16$$
$$1.5\times IQR=24$$
$$\text{Upper bound}=106+24=130,\quad\text{Lower bound}=90-24=66$$
$\therefore$ Charlie is not an outlier in the new club, as his score is not outside the bounds $66$ to $130$.
criteria: Finds the range of Charlie's score between $98$ and $130$, or equivalent merit
Finds the IQR of either club, or equivalent merit

Tom invests \$750 at the end of each quarter into an account which earns $8\%$ per annum with interest compounded quarterly.

He does this for 3 years.

Find the future value of Tom's investment.
